prompt: Which part of Expo is a paid service, with a free allowance?

choices.text: The SDK
choices.why: The SDK is open source libraries.

choices.text: Prebuild
choices.why: Prebuild runs on your computer, free.

choices.text: EAS
choices.why: Right: builds, updates and submissions in Expo's cloud.

choices.text: The command-line tools you run with `npx expo`
choices.why: The CLI is open source and runs locally.

prompt: You ask `npx expo install` for `expo-camera` in an SDK 58 project. Which version does it install?

choices.text: The one that belongs to SDK 58
choices.why: Right: the version tested with React Native 0.88 and the rest of that release.

choices.text: The newest version published on npm
choices.why: That is what `npm install` does; `expo install` looks up the SDK's table first.

choices.text: Whichever version the phone's Expo Go has
choices.why: The phone is not consulted; the project's SDK decides.

choices.text: The oldest version that still compiles
choices.why: Nothing chooses by age.

prompt: A 2019 tutorial says you must eject from Expo to add native code. What is true today?

choices.text: Ejecting is still required, but it is now called prebuild
choices.why: Prebuild generates the folders and can run again; ejecting was a one-way conversion.

choices.text: Expo projects still cannot contain native code
choices.why: They can: a library's or your own, through plugins and modules.

choices.text: Native code is allowed only in Expo's paid plans
choices.why: Native code has nothing to do with paying.

choices.text: An Expo project holds native code, and nobody ejects
choices.why: Right: the managed/bare split and ejecting describe Expo before 2021.

prompt: In a bare project, a new permission has to reach both platforms. What does the change involve?

choices.text: One line in `app.json`
choices.why: That is the Expo way; a bare project has no generation step to apply it.

choices.text: An edit to `AndroidManifest.xml` and another to `Info.plist`, kept in agreement by you
choices.why: Right: two files in two formats, and nothing checks they match.

choices.text: Nothing: React Native asks for permissions on its own
choices.why: Every permission is declared in each native project.

choices.text: A change to `package.json`
choices.why: npm's file knows nothing about permissions.

prompt: Your bare project is four React Native versions behind. Why is upgrading slow work?

choices.text: npm cannot skip versions and installs each one in turn
choices.why: npm installs the version you ask for directly.

choices.text: The native template changed in each, and you apply its diff to files you have since edited
choices.why: Right: that is what the upgrade helper shows, and nobody can apply it for you.

choices.text: Each version needs a newer Mac
choices.why: The Android half has nothing to do with Macs, and the delay is the same there.

choices.text: The stores must approve each intermediate version
choices.why: The stores never see versions you do not publish.

prompt: A payment SDK ships Kotlin and Swift code and is not part of the Expo SDK. Why does it fail in Expo Go?

choices.text: Expo Go blocks payments by policy
choices.why: No such policy; the cause is the native code.

choices.text: Its JavaScript is too large for Expo Go to download
choices.why: Size is not the problem.

choices.text: Expo Go runs only on iOS
choices.why: It is in both stores.

choices.text: Its native code was never compiled into Expo Go
choices.why: Right: Expo Go only contains the native code it was built with.

prompt: Match each situation with where you would run the app.

pairs.left: first day, only Expo SDK libraries
a native library outside the SDK
checking a component's logic with no phone

prompt: What does `expo-dev-client` add to your own build of the app?

choices.text: Loading JavaScript from the dev server, as Expo Go does
choices.why: Right: that turns your build into your own Expo Go.

choices.text: The camera module, compiled in ahead of time
choices.why: That is `expo-camera`.

choices.text: A licence to publish in the stores
choices.why: Publishing is between you and each store.

choices.text: An emulator
choices.why: The emulator comes with the Android SDK.

prompt: In a prebuild project, where should the Android package name be written?

choices.text: In `android/app/build.gradle`
choices.why: That file is output: the next `prebuild --clean` rewrites it.

choices.text: In `package.json`, as the `name` field
choices.why: npm's name is not the store identity.

choices.text: In `app.json`
choices.why: Right: in `expo.android.package`, and prebuild writes it into Gradle.

choices.text: In `.gitignore`
choices.why: That file only lists what git skips.

prompt: A teammate fixed a build problem by editing `android/gradle.properties` by hand. It worked until yesterday. What most plausibly happened?

choices.text: Someone ran `prebuild --clean`
choices.why: Right: that regenerated the folder without the edit. Generated folders are output, and a change belongs in a plugin.

choices.text: Expo Go overwrote the file on the phone
choices.why: Expo Go never sees your native folders.

choices.text: The edit needed a paid EAS plan
choices.why: Local files do not depend on a plan.

choices.text: Gradle forgets settings after a week
choices.why: Gradle keeps whatever is in the file.

prompt: Expo calls generating the native folders from configuration Continuous Native ___.
When does a config plugin run?

choices.text: Every time the app opens on the phone
choices.why: It is gone by then; it only ever edited files.

choices.text: When Metro bundles the JavaScript
choices.why: Metro bundles code; plugins change native files.

choices.text: During prebuild, while the native projects are written
choices.why: Right: in Node.js on your computer.

choices.text: Only inside EAS Build, on Expo's own servers in the cloud
choices.why: EAS runs prebuild like your computer does, and so does `npx expo prebuild`.

prompt: Two plugins insert lines into `AndroidManifest.xml`. One uses `withAndroidManifest`; the other finds `</application>` with a regular expression and pastes text before it. Which is fragile, and why?

choices.text: The first, because parsed XML loses comments
choices.why: Losing a comment does not break a build.

choices.text: The second, which relies on the template's exact text
choices.why: Right; the helper works on the parsed file whatever its layout.

choices.text: Neither of them, since prebuild validates every change it applies
choices.why: Prebuild applies changes; it cannot tell a misplaced one.

choices.text: Both, because plugins cannot touch the manifest
choices.why: Touching the manifest is what `withAndroidManifest` exists for.

prompt: Put the steps of adding a native setting through a plugin in order.
React Native 0.89 comes out tomorrow with a fix you need. Your app is on Expo SDK 58. What is the realistic path?

choices.text: Nothing: Expo upgrades React Native inside the phone automatically
choices.why: React Native is compiled into your app; an update cannot change it, as lesson 21 explains.

choices.text: Install 0.89 with npm and keep every Expo library as it is
choices.why: The SDK 58 libraries were tested against 0.88, not 0.89.

choices.text: Pay for an EAS plan, which includes early React Native versions
choices.why: No plan changes which React Native an SDK supports.

choices.text: Wait for the SDK built on 0.89, or patch the package meanwhile
choices.why: Right: an SDK release pairs with one React Native version.

prompt: Match each EAS service with its local alternative.

pairs.right: your own server speaking the update protocol

prompt: Which situation points to starting a bare project?

choices.text: A new app that will use the camera and location
choices.why: Both are in the Expo SDK, with plugins.

choices.text: A new app built by a team that knows only JavaScript
choices.why: That is the case Expo serves best.

choices.text: An existing native app adding React Native to two screens
choices.why: Right: the native project already exists and belongs to its team.

choices.text: Any app that needs to keep working offline, away from a network
choices.why: Offline work is JavaScript and storage, in either kind of project.

prompt: A team generates its native folders, and one developer now needs a custom Xcode build phase. Which choice keeps prebuild working?

choices.text: Write a config plugin that adds the phase
choices.why: Right: the change is then applied every time the folder is generated.

choices.text: Add the phase in Xcode and commit `ios/`, still running `prebuild --clean` as before
choices.why: The next clean prebuild deletes the phase.

choices.text: Move the phase into `App.tsx`
choices.why: A build phase is Xcode's, not JavaScript's.

choices.text: Ask Expo Go to run the phase
choices.why: Expo Go never builds your project.

prompt: Which of these change when you set `expo.android.package` and run prebuild? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: `applicationId` in the Android Gradle file
choices.why: Yes, the capture showed it.

choices.text: The name of the npm package
choices.why: `package.json` is untouched.

choices.text: The iOS bundle identifier
choices.why: That is a separate field, `expo.ios.bundleIdentifier`.

choices.text: The identity the Play Store will know the app by
choices.why: Yes: the package name is that identity.

prompt: How much does it take to turn a prebuild project into a bare one?

choices.text: Rewriting the app in Kotlin and Swift
choices.why: The JavaScript stays exactly as it is.

choices.text: A paid migration service
choices.why: Nothing needs paying.

choices.text: It cannot be done once Expo is installed
choices.why: It is one commit, and the Expo libraries keep working.

choices.text: Generate the folders and commit them
choices.why: Right, and removing them from `.gitignore`.
